title: Speaking practice: Opinions, Causes, and Comparisons
description: Eight speaking tasks. Students choose a story title, report a lost lunch box, give a Friday choice, explain why towns grow beside rivers, compare notebook prices, teach about solids, liquids, and gases, give an opinion about a story, and explain a character's change. Students record two takes; teachers or students review the recordings.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Read this very short story.
A little cloud wanted to be a big storm cloud. It tried to be loud, but it only made a tiny sound. Then it rained gently on a dry garden. The flowers opened up, and the cloud felt proud.
Here are two possible titles. Title 1: “The Loud Little Cloud.” Title 2: “The Cloud That Helped the Garden.”
Tell your teacher which title is better for the story.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: You cannot find your lunch box. You go to the front office to ask for help. Here is what happened today.
In the morning, you carried your lunch box onto the school bus. You put it on the seat next to you.
At school, you got off the bus and ran to class. You forgot the lunch box on the seat.
Now it is almost lunch time, and you cannot find it.
Tell the office helper what happened and ask for help.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your teacher says the class can choose one fun activity on Friday afternoon. The choices are a game hour or a drawing hour.
Your teacher asks each student to choose one and give a reason.
Tell your teacher your choice and why.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Many towns and cities are built beside rivers. Look at these facts.
Rivers give people fresh water to drink and to water crops.
Boats can carry people and goods on a river.
The land near a river is often flat and has rich soil for farming.
Fish live in rivers, and people can catch them for food.
Explain to a classmate why people choose to build towns near rivers.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: A store sells notebooks in two packs.
Pack A: 2 notebooks for $6.
Pack B: 5 notebooks for $10.
Priya says, “Pack B costs more money, so it is not a good deal.” Maria says, “Pack B is the better deal.”
Tell a friend who is right. Use math to show how you know.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your class made a chart about three things. Use the chart to teach a younger student about solids, liquids, and gases.
Wooden block (solid): keeps its own shape. You can hold it in your hand.
Orange juice (liquid): flows and takes the shape of its cup. You can pour it.
Air in a balloon (gas): spreads out to fill the whole balloon. You cannot see it.
Teach the younger student what makes each kind of matter different.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Read this part of a story. Yuki accidentally breaks a classroom window with a ball at recess. Nobody saw her. The teacher asks the class, “Does anyone know who broke the window?” Yuki is afraid of getting in trouble. Her best friend whispers, “Don’t say anything.”
Your book club is talking about the story. Give your opinion about what Yuki should do and why. Also say one reason why someone might disagree with you.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Read this part of a story. Rafi was afraid to read aloud in class. His voice shook, and his hands felt cold. At home, he practiced with his little sister, who clapped every time he finished a page. By Friday, Rafi stood up in class, took a deep breath, and read the whole page. His voice was steady, and he felt proud.
Your reading group wants to talk about how the character changed. Explain what made the change happen.

items.stem: Choose the better title for the story about the little cloud and tell why.

checklist: I said which title I choose.
I gave a reason from the story.
I used the word because.
I said one thing that happens in the story.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: chooses one title and gives at least one reason connected to the story.
Evidence: names a story event (the rain, the dry garden, the tiny sound) that fits the title.
Sentence-level language: because connecting the choice and the reason; mostly complete sentences.
Clarity: clear enough for a teacher to understand the choice and the reason.

support.clue: Read the title choices. Which one matches the most important part of the story? Find one event that proves it.
support.frame: I think Title ______ is better because ______. In the story, ______. That is why ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a different story: “I think ‘The Boy and the Blue Boat’ is a better title than ‘A Rainy Day’ because the boat is in most parts of the story. In the story, the boy builds a boat and sails it across the pond. That is why the title with the boat fits.” Now choose the better title for the cloud story.

items.stem: Tell the office helper what happened to your lunch box.

checklist: I told what I did in the morning.
I told what I forgot.
I used past-tense verbs (carried, put, forgot).
I politely asked for help.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: tells the sequence (carried it on, put it on the seat, forgot it) and makes a request for help.
Organization: events in order from morning to now.
Sentence-level language: past-tense verbs, time words (this morning, then, now), and a polite request (Can you help me, please?).
Register: polite tone suited to a school helper.

support.clue: Think about three parts: this morning, when you got to school, and now. Then add a polite question.
support.frame: This morning, I ______. I put my lunch box ______. Then I ______. Now ______. Can you help me ______?
support.model: Mentor example. About a broken bike light: “This morning, I rode my bike to school. I locked it at the rack. Then I went to class. Now the front light is hanging by a wire. Can you help me find someone to fix it, please?” Now tell the office helper about your lunch box.

items.stem: Tell your teacher which Friday activity you choose, a game hour or a drawing hour, and give a reason.

checklist: I said which activity I choose.
I gave a reason.
I gave an example to explain my reason.
I used because.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states a clear choice and at least one reason.
Elaboration: adds an example or detail that explains the reason (for example, who it helps, what they would do).
Sentence-level language: because connecting choice and reason; polite phrasing (I would like).
Clarity: choice and reason are easy for a teacher to follow.

support.clue: Think about what you like and why. Then think of one example of what you would do during the activity.
support.frame: I would like the ______ because ______. For example, ______. I think it would be fun for the class because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About an outdoor lesson: “I would like to read outside because the shade is cool. For example, we could sit under the big tree. I think it would be calm for the class because there is more space.” Now tell your teacher your Friday choice.

items.stem: Explain why many towns were built near rivers, using the facts on the list.

checklist: I gave at least two reasons.
I used the facts from the list.
I used because, so, or since to link a reason to the result.
I used a closing sentence.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: explains at least two reasons from the list and links them to the choice of building near rivers.
Cause and effect: connects each reason (water, transport, soil, food) to why people settle there.
Organization: introduces the idea, gives reasons, and closes with a summary.
Sentence-level language: connectors of reason and result (because, so, since, as a result).
Vocabulary: crops, goods, soil, and farming used accurately.

support.clue: Read the four facts. For each one, ask: how does this help people live in a town?
support.frame: Many towns were built near rivers because ______. First, ______. Also, ______. As a result, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a bus station: “Many shops open near a bus station because many people pass by. First, workers can buy lunch quickly. Also, travelers need water and snacks. As a result, more shops want to open there.” Now explain why people built towns near rivers.

facts: Rivers provide fresh water for drinking and for crops.
Boats can carry people and goods on rivers.
Land near rivers often has rich soil good for farming.
Rivers have fish that people can catch for food.

items.stem: Decide whether Priya or Maria is right about which notebook pack is the better deal, and explain with numbers.

checklist: I said who is right.
I found the cost of one notebook in each pack.
I used the numbers $6, $10, 2, and 5.
I used words like each, per notebook, or cost less.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: concludes that Maria is right and supports it with the cost of one notebook in each pack.
Mathematical reasoning: finds $3 per notebook for Pack A (6 ÷ 2) and $2 per notebook for Pack B (10 ÷ 5) and compares them.
Vocabulary: each, per, cost, and total used accurately.
Sentence-level language: comparison language (cheaper than, costs less for each) and reasoning (so, therefore, because).
Clarity: names the operation or the idea of sharing the price equally.

support.clue: A bigger total price does not tell you which pack is cheaper for one notebook. How can you find the price of just one notebook in each pack?
support.frame: I think ______ is right because ______. In Pack A, $______ divided by ______ notebooks is $______ each. In Pack B, $______ divided by ______ notebooks is $______ each. So Pack ______ costs less for each notebook.
support.model: Mentor example. About juice boxes: “Pack A has 4 juice boxes for $8, and Pack B has 6 juice boxes for $18. Pack A costs $8 ÷ 4 = $2 for each juice box. Pack B costs $18 ÷ 6 = $3 for each juice box. So Pack A is the better deal because each juice box costs less.” Now decide about the notebooks.

facts: $6 ÷ 2 = $3 for each notebook in Pack A
$10 ÷ 5 = $2 for each notebook in Pack B
$2 is less than $3, so Pack B is the better deal

items.stem: Tell a younger student how a solid, a liquid, and a gas are different, using the chart.

checklist: I told about a solid, a liquid, and a gas.
I used an example from the chart for each one.
I told how they are different from each other.
I used simple words that a younger student can understand.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: describes all three states with an accurate property for each.
Organization: one state at a time, plus a closing comparison or contrast.
Vocabulary: solid, liquid, gas, shape, and fill used accurately.
Sentence-level language: contrast phrases (but, however, unlike) and descriptive noun groups.
Audience awareness: language suited to a younger listener.

support.clue: Look at each row of the chart. Ask: what happens to its shape? Then compare the three rows.
support.frame: A solid ______. A liquid ______. A gas ______. They are different because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About clouds, rain, and snow: “Rain falls as drops of water. Snow falls as soft, white flakes. Clouds are made of tiny drops that float in the sky. They are different because they look and feel different.” Now teach the younger student about solids, liquids, and gases.

facts: A solid keeps its own shape.
A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
A gas spreads out to fill its container.

items.stem: Tell whether Yuki should tell the truth about the broken window, and support your opinion with reasons from the story.

checklist: I said what Yuki should do.
I gave two reasons that use details from the story.
I said why someone might disagree.
I used although, however, or on the other hand.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states an opinion, gives two reasons, and acknowledges a different point of view.
Evidence: uses story details (nobody saw her, she is afraid, her friend whispered, the teacher asked).
Organization: opinion, reasons, other view, and a closing statement.
Sentence-level language: complex sentences with although or even though; modal verbs (should, could).
Elaboration: explains the effects of the choice on Yuki, the teacher, or the class.

support.clue: Find the details that make the choice hard for Yuki. Think about what could happen if she tells and if she does not tell.
support.frame: I think Yuki should ______ because ______. Also, ______. In the story, ______. Although some people may say ______, I think ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a found wallet: “I think Ravi should give the wallet to the teacher because it belongs to someone else. Also, the owner may need the money. In the story, Ravi sees a name inside. Although some people may say it is only a small amount of money, I think he should return it.” Now give your opinion about Yuki.

items.stem: Explain what caused Rafi to feel more confident about reading aloud by Friday.

checklist: I told how Rafi felt at the beginning and at the end.
I told what caused the change.
I used details from the story as evidence.
I used because, so, or as a result.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: contrasts Rafi's feelings at the beginning and the end and identifies practice and encouragement as the causes of the change.
Evidence: uses story details (shaking voice, practicing with his sister, her clapping, steady voice).
Organization: before, cause, after.
Sentence-level language: cause-and-effect connectors (because, so, as a result, which made him) in complex sentences.
Vocabulary: feeling and trait words such as afraid, nervous, confident, and proud.

support.clue: Compare how Rafi feels at the beginning with how he feels on Friday. Then find what he did in between.
support.frame: At the beginning, Rafi felt ______ because ______. Then he ______. His sister ______, which made him feel ______. As a result, by Friday, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a runner: “At the beginning, Dalia felt tired because she could not finish a lap. Then she ran a little farther each day. Her coach cheered for her, which made her feel strong. As a result, by the end of the month, she ran four laps.” Now explain what changed for Rafi.
